web_title: 7. Why the Price Is What It Is: Valuation, Reverse DCF & Peer Comps
book_title: Chapter 7: What the Market Is Pricing In at $398.73
question: What future free cash flow growth and terminal multiple are embedded in TSM's $1,976.82B enterprise value, and why does the market discount its 17.26x forward P/E?

epigraph.quote: Price is what you pay; value is what you get. In capital-intensive monopolies, the spread between the two is governed by the capex cycle.
epigraph.author: Institutional Underwriting Principle

web_blocks.text: Deconstructing the $398.73 Price Tag & Multiple Compression

web_blocks.html: At the November 13, 2026 close of $398.73, TSMC (NYSE: TSM) carries a $2,068.01 billion market cap on Finviz ($1,844.69B on TradingView ADR count) [21]. Its enterprise value stands at $1,976.82 billion [21]. On trailing results ($156.42B sales, $80.58B net income), TSM trades at 25.66x trailing P/E and 17.34x EV/EBITDA [21]. It also trades at 12.64x EV/Sales and 9.41x price-to-book [21]. Looking ahead, consensus places TSM at 17.26x forward P/E and a 0.42 PEG ratio against a $554.22 Street target (+39.0% upside) [21].

On the surface, paying 17.26x forward earnings for 64.77% gross margins, 57.78% operating margins, 32.67% ROIC, and 41.98% ROE looks cheap [21]. Q3 2026 sales grew +41.2% YoY and October sales jumped +59.7% YoY [5, 6]. Yet the market rarely prices a $2 trillion company at 17x forward earnings by accident. Three discounts sit inside the $398.73 quote. First, FY2026 capex is surging to $60B–$64B, depressing near-term FCF conversion [4]. Second, ramping Arizona Fab 21, Kumamoto JASM, and Dresden ESMC brings 2%–4% gross margin dilution [10, 13]. Third, Taiwan Strait geopolitical risk pairs with a 5.10% U.S. 10-year Treasury yield [28].

web_blocks.text: Reverse DCF: What $1,976.82B Enterprise Value Demands

web_blocks.html: To strip away narrative bias, we invert the valuation. We use a 9.5% WACC—based on a 5.10% risk-free rate [28], ~1.1x beta, and a 100 bps Taiwan premium—plus 3.5% terminal growth. At those inputs, a $1,976.82B EV requires FCF to compound from $31.96B in FY2025 to $115B–$130B by Year 10. That model also assumes a depressed FY2026E capex trough and a 16x–18x terminal EV/FCF multiple.

web_blocks.how_calculated: Solved for the 10-year FCF compounding rate that equates discounted FCF (Years 1–10) plus terminal value (Year 10 FCF / (WACC - g)) to EV of $1,976.82B.
web_blocks.the_inputs: EV = $1,976.82B; FY2025 FCF = $31.96B; TTM Net Income = $80.58B; TTM Sales = $156.42B; WACC = 9.5% (US10Y 5.10% + equity & geopolitical risk); Terminal g = 3.5% (16.7x terminal FCF).
web_blocks.the_range: 11.5% CAGR if capex intensity normalizes from ~40% of sales back to 28% by 2029 (releasing $130B+ FCF); 16.5% CAGR if capex stays permanently above 35% of sales.
web_blocks.if_off: If AI hyperscaler capex digestion forces utilization below 75% in 2028 while depreciation from $60B+ annual capex hits COGS, FCF stalls near $45B–$55B and fair EV compresses toward $1,350B–$1,500B (~$275–$305/share).

web_blocks.html: FY2025 FCF of $31.96B understates steady-state owner earnings because $40.5B+ of growth capex was front-loaded for N2 and CoWoS [1, 4, 20]. On $80.58B of TTM net income, the market implies only ~7%–8% annual owner-earnings growth over ten years. That is a low bar when Q4 2026 guidance ($52.3B–$54.3B) points to >$210B annualized sales [5]. The catch is that if AI capex proves cyclical, TSMC's fixed depreciation ($688B NT / ~$21.5B USD in FY2025, and rising) will amplify any revenue dip [11].

web_blocks.takeaway: At 25.66x trailing and 17.26x forward P/E, TSM trades near its 2024–2025 trailing average but at a clear forward discount. Still, it sits well above the 11.2x–11.9x trough reached during the 2022 rate and inventory shock.

web_blocks.text: Peer Comparison: Merchant Monopoly vs. Trailing Foundries & Equipment

web_blocks.caption: TSM vs. Foundry & Lithography Peers (Market Snapshot as of 2026-11-13)
web_blocks.takeaway: TSM delivers 41.98% ROE at 25.66x trailing P/E (17.26x forward), while UMC (19.83% ROE, 14.65x P/E) and GFS (1.67% ROE, 119.96x P/E) stay in mature nodes. INTC (-10.87% ROE) bleeds foundry cash, and only ASML (65.98% ROE, 36.83x P/E) shares TSM's monopoly economics at a ~43% higher trailing multiple.

web_blocks.html: The peer table shows why TSMC has no true public-market substitute [26]. United Microelectronics (UMC, $15.40, $38.52B cap) trades at 14.65x trailing and 13.70x forward P/E after exiting nodes below 14nm [26]. Its 19.83% ROE is solid, yet UMC is a mature-node price-taker down -46.82% from its 52-week high [26]. GlobalFoundries (GFS, $41.47, $22.76B cap) trades at 119.96x trailing P/E (16.13x forward) with a 1.67% ROE after quitting 7nm in 2018 [19, 26]. Intel (INTC, $59.66, $317.09B cap) stays loss-making (-10.87% ROE, 33.02x forward P/E, 0.44x D/E) and down -58.09% from highs on 18A losses [17, 26]. Only ASML ($1,495.16, $565.30B cap) matches TSMC's monopoly power with 65.98% ROE, trading at 36.83x trailing and 23.55x forward P/E—a 43% trailing premium to TSM [26].

web_blocks.region_era: Korea / U.S. Semiconductor Memory & Capex Cycles (2018–2023)
web_blocks.mechanism: In the 2017–2018 and 2021–2022 upcycles, memory leaders posted 50%+ gross margins and looked cheap at 6x–10x trailing P/E. Then hyperscaler inventory digestion and heavy capex collided with rising depreciation.
web_blocks.outcome_numbers: In 2022–2023, Micron's sales dropped 49% YoY ($30.8B to $15.5B) and gross margin swung from +45% to -9%. Samsung's Device Solutions unit posted multi-billion-dollar losses despite looking cheap on peak multiples.
web_blocks.lesson_for_symbol: TSMC's foundry model has far stronger lock-in and pricing power than commodity memory. Still, the trap is similar: low forward P/Es can compress further if $60B+ capex meets even a brief hyperscaler pause.

web_blocks.text: Capex Intensity vs. Owner Earnings Bridge

web_blocks.html: Valuing FY2025 FCF ($31.96B) as a permanent ceiling is a common mistake; it is a mid-buildout trough. In FY2025, TSMC generated $72.52B in operating cash flow and spent ~$40.5B on capex (33.1% of sales) [1, 20]. With FY2026 capex guided to $60B–$64B on ~$175B–$180B in sales, capex intensity briefly rises to ~35% [4, 5]. Maintenance capex for 17M+ wafers is only ~$18B–$22B a year, so ~$40B+ is discretionary growth spend for N2, A16, and CoWoS [4, 9]. Normalized owner earnings (CFO minus maintenance capex) already top $60B–$70B, implying ~28x–32x today or ~18x–20x FY2027E earnings.

web_blocks.title: The Geopolitical & Rate Discount Factor
paragraphs: Why doesn't TSM trade at ASML's 36.83x trailing P/E [26]? Over 85% of leading-edge capacity sits in Taiwan, adding a geopolitical discount despite Arizona, Kumamoto, and Dresden expansions [13]. A 5.10% U.S. 10-year Treasury yield also lifts the equity hurdle [28]. At 5.10% risk-free, investors demand a ~5.8% forward earnings yield (17.26x P/E) rather than the 28x–31x P/E seen in the 2020–2021 zero-rate era [22].

web_blocks.html: At $398.73 (25.66x trailing P/E, 17.26x forward P/E, 0.42 PEG, 17.34x EV/EBITDA), valuation reflects a clear tug-of-war [21]. World-class fundamentals (64.77% gross margin, 32.67% ROIC) battle real overhangs: $60B–$64B FY26 capex, 2%–4% overseas dilution, and a 5.10% US10Y [4, 10, 21, 28]. Against UMC, GFS, INTC, and ASML (36.83x trailing P/E), TSM is attractively priced—especially in the $369.38–$380.64 support zone.

TSMC's 32.67% ROIC against a 9.5% WACC creates a >23% economic spread [21]. That spread justifies a lasting premium over mature foundries like UMC and GFS, even while Stage 4 technicals cap near-term multiples [21, 26].

book_paragraphs: With business quality established, we must ask the key investing question: what are we paying on November 13, 2026? At $398.73 per ADR, TSMC carries a $1,976.82 billion enterprise value. For a company growing quarterly sales above 40% YoY, the multiples look modest: 25.66x trailing P/E, 17.26x forward P/E, and a 0.42 PEG against a $554.22 Street target.

When a $2 trillion monopoly trades at 17x forward earnings with 64.77% gross margins and 32.67% ROIC, we ask what worries the market. Three real frictions explain the discount. First, 2026 capex is jumping to $60B–$64B, squeezing near-term FCF ($31.96B in FY25) below $80.58B in trailing net income. Second, ramping fabs in Arizona, Kumamoto, and Dresden will trim 2 to 4 points off gross margin. Third, a 5.10% 10-year Treasury yield and Taiwan risk demand a wider equity premium.

Let us examine the bridge between accounting profit and owner earnings. Critics cite the gap between $80.58B in trailing net income and $31.96B in FY25 FCF as proof of a capital treadmill. That ignores the split between maintenance and growth capex. Keeping 17 million wafers running takes $18B–$22B a year; the other $40B+ in FY26 builds new 2nm and CoWoS capacity.

Adjusting for front-loaded growth spend, normalized owner earnings already top $60B per year. At a $1.98 trillion EV, the market asks 17.26x forward earnings—below mega-cap software peers despite 41%+ sales growth and 32.67% ROIC. That discount persists because investors demand pay for Taiwan concentration and a 5.10% Treasury yield.

book_callouts.title: The Reverse DCF Reality Check
book_callouts.text: At a 9.5% discount rate and 3.5% terminal growth, a $1.98 trillion EV implies ~13.5% to 15.0% annual FCF growth over ten years from FY2025's $31.96B base. That is achievable if capex cools after 2027, but vulnerable if AI spending pauses as $60B+ capex turns into depreciation.

book_subsections.title: Why Peers Offer No Escape—and What History Warns About Cycle Multiples
paragraphs: Across semiconductor manufacturing on November 13, 2026, TSMC's valuation looks compelling against peers. UMC trades at 14.65x trailing earnings after leaving leading-edge nodes. GlobalFoundries trades near 120x trailing earnings with a 1.67% ROE. Intel posts -10.87% ROE and trades at 33.02x forward earnings while burning cash on foundry ramps. Only ASML shares true monopoly economics at 36.83x trailing and 23.55x forward earnings, even in its own Stage 4 downtrend.

Yet history warns against confusing a low forward P/E with a guaranteed floor in chip hardware. In 2022, rate hikes and PC/mobile destocking pushed TSMC's trailing P/E down to 11.2x and EV/EBITDA below 8x. Memory giants Micron and Samsung also looked cheap on single-digit P/Es right before the 2022–2023 bust wiped out margins. TSMC has far stronger lock-in and pricing power, so it deserves a premium—but valuation alone will not halt a Stage 4 tape at 5.10% yields.

book_subsections.title: Sensitivity Check: Where Valuation Becomes Undeniable
paragraphs: If TSM pulls back to our $369.38–$380.64 support zone, forward P/E drops to ~16.0x–16.5x and EV falls by $95B–$150B. The Reverse DCF hurdle eases to 11.5%–12.5% FCF growth, giving long-term buyers a wide margin of safety even with 300 bps of overseas dilution. Conversely, a 2022-style shock (11.2x–14.0x trailing P/E) warns that price can overshoot downward, making technical confirmation and a hard stop essential.

book_subsections.title: How Multiples Drive the 12-Month Return Distribution
paragraphs: The sensitivity table makes the math clear. At $398.73 and 17.26x forward earnings, consensus already models ~$23.10 in forward EPS. Reaching our $485.00 Base target does not require heroic multiples—just $23.80 EPS and a 20.4x P/E, well below TSM's 2020–2021 peak (28x–31x) and ASML's 23.55x forward P/E.

On the downside, an AI capex pause that trims forward EPS to $21.50 at 13.5x puts the stock at our $290.00 Bear case (inside our $275–$305 Reverse DCF bear range). Buying at $369.38–$380.64 with a $348.00 stop below the $351.19 swing low delivers a 3.20:1 payoff.

book_subsections.title: Valuation Summary: Fair Today, Asymmetric at Support
paragraphs: At $398.73, TSMC is neither a bubble nor a risk-free bargain. It is a modestly discounted monopoly whose 17.26x forward P/E already prices in slower 2027 growth and overseas dilution. Waiting for $369.38–$380.64 simply tilts the odds further in our favor.

book_subsections.title: Economic Spread: ROIC vs. Cost of Capital
paragraphs: Valuation ultimately rests on the spread between ROIC and cost of capital. Earning 32.67% ROIC against a 9.5% WACC means every dollar reinvested into N2 and CoWoS cleanrooms creates huge economic value—so long as end-demand absorbs the capacity.

book_subsections.title: Why Forward Multiples Matter More Than Trailing P/E in Capex Inflections
paragraphs: In a heavy node-transition year like 2026, trailing multiples mislead investors. When TSMC spends $60B to $64B in one year for 2nm and CoWoS, depreciation hits the P&L before new fabs reach full output. Tracking 17.26x forward earnings and normalized owner earnings corrects that mismatch and shows why institutions step in when forward P/Es dip into the mid-teens.

book_subsections.title: Step-by-Step Reverse DCF: Walking Through the $1,976.82B Math
paragraphs: Let us walk through the Reverse DCF math together so you and I see every assumption clearly. We start with TSM's $1,976.82 billion enterprise value at the $398.73 close. Against that price tag, FY2025 free cash flow was $31.96 billion. You and I then set a 9.5% discount rate, built from the 5.10% 10-year Treasury yield, a 1.1x beta, and a 100 bps Taiwan risk premium. Add a 3.5% terminal growth rate, which implies a 16.7x terminal FCF multiple.

Now solve backward for the cash flow growth required to justify $1,976.82 billion. From $31.96 billion in FY2025, FCF must compound at 13.5% to 15.0% annually for ten years, reaching $115 billion to $130 billion by Year 10. That sounds steep until you and I separate maintenance capex from growth capex. Keeping 17 million wafers running takes $18 billion to $22 billion each year. Meanwhile, FY2026 capex surges to $60B–$64B for N2 and CoWoS. Once that buildout cools after 2027, normalized owner earnings above $60 billion make a 17.26x forward P/E and 0.42 PEG look very forgiving. You and I are not paying for perfection here; we are paying for steady execution.

book_subsections.title: You and I vs. the Peer Group: Why TSM Dwarfs Foundries Yet Trails ASML
paragraphs: Next, you and I compare TSM's 32.67% ROIC and 57.78% operating margin against every public peer. UMC trades at 14.65x trailing earnings with a 19.83% ROE, but it exited leading-edge nodes below 14nm and competes on price. GlobalFoundries trades at 119.96x trailing earnings while earning just a 1.67% ROE after quitting 7nm in 2018. Intel posts a -10.87% ROE and trades at 33.02x forward earnings as 18A losses weigh on cash flow.

Only ASML shares TSM's monopoly economics, posting a 65.98% ROE while trading at 36.83x trailing earnings and 23.55x forward earnings. Why does ASML command a 43% trailing premium over TSM's 25.66x trailing and 17.26x forward P/E? Over 85% of TSM's leading-edge capacity sits in Taiwan. In addition, overseas fabs in Arizona, Kumamoto, and Dresden trim 2% to 4% off gross margin. That valuation gap gives you and I a clear benchmark: TSM already prices in heavy caution relative to its 64.77% gross margin.
